title: ‘Drunk History’ Returns With New Short-Form Episodes 7 Years After Comedy Central Finale
description:
After a long hangover, “Drunk History” is back.

	The Emmy-winning comedy show is returning with three new short-form episodes, seven years after it
body:
After a long hangover, “Drunk History” is back.

	The Emmy-winning comedy show is returning with three new short-form episodes, seven years after it last aired on Comedy Central.

	From Derek Waters and Jeremy Konner, “Drunk History” pairs inebriated storytellers with scrappy historical reenactments. (The facts and dates are true, but the dialogue definitely isn’t.) The first new episode, launching on Sept. 15 on Comedy Central’s YouTube channel, stars Meghan Trainor as Madonna, focusing on the pop icon’s legendary performance at the inaugural VMAs.
	

	The cast also includes Steve Agee, Tim Baltz, Seth Green, Colin Hanks, Jack McBrayer, Chris Parnell, Johnny Pemberton, Daryl Sabara, Mae Whitman, Weird “Al” Yankovic and more, with narrators including Lisa Gilroy, Patton Oswalt and Marisha Ray.


	The other storylines center on Frances Perkins (the unsung architect of FDR’s New Deal) and two men’s lifelong battle to make the world’s largest ball of twine.

	“Drunk History” started in 2007 as a Funny or Die web series before Comedy Central picked it up as a TV show that ran for six seasons from 2013 to 2019. That year, the network renewed “Drunk History” for a seventh season but reversed the decision in 2020, when production was halted due to the pandemic.

	Guest stars over the years include Jack Black, Will Ferrell, Bill Hader, Kristen Wiig, Lin-Manuel Miranda, Bob Odenkirk and more.

	“I’m so excited to be back making Drunk History again! We have a lot of catching up to do,” said Waters.  

	“We are thrilled that ‘Drunk History’ is back,” said Ari Pearce, head of Comedy Central original content. “These new episodes reflect our heritage as both the home of iconic comedy franchises and a premier launchpad for comedic talent. As we continue to expand our reach across platforms, ‘Drunk History’ is a great example of how we’re delivering Comedy Central to fans in new ways.”

schema.headline: ‘Drunk History’ Returns With New Short-Form Episodes 7 Years After Comedy Central Finale

title: Mo’Nique Signs With Innovative
description: Mo’Nique has signed with Innovative Artists Entertainment for representation in all areas, Variety has learned. She continues to be repped by attorn
body:
Mo’Nique has signed with Innovative Artists Entertainment for representation in all areas, Variety has learned. She continues to be repped by attorney Ricky Anderson and manager Sidney Hicks. 

	Mo’Nique first broke out as a stand up comic, including being one of the stars of the stand up film “The Queens of Comedy.” She earned a Grammy nomination for best spoken comedy album for the film. She also made notable appearances on shows like “Showtime at the Apollo” and “Def Comedy Jam.” Her stand up specials include “I Could Have Been Your Cellmate” and “Mo’Nique & Friends: Live from Atlanta” for Showtime and “My Name is Mo’Nique” for Netflix. 
	

	As an actor, Mo’Nique is best known for her critically-acclaimed role in the hit film “Precious: Based on the Novel ‘Push’ by Sapphire.” She was nominated for and won the Academy Award for best supporting actress, as well as a Golden Globe, Screen Actors Guild Award, Critics’ Choice Award, BAFTA Award, and Image Award, among many other accolades. 


	She also appeared in films like “Domino,” “Farce of the Penguins,” “Beerfest,” and “Phat Girlz.” She recently appeared in “The Deliverance” for Netflix, which reunited her with Lee Daniels. 

	In television, Mo’Nique appeared in multiple episodes of “Moesha,” which led to her starring in the hit spinoff series “The Parkers” for five seasons. She also played the same character, Nikki Parker, in “The Hughleys.” She also hosted the BET talk show “The Mo’Nique Show” for two seasons and over 250 episodes. Her other TV roles include “Black Mafia Family,” the HBO movie “Bessie,” and “Ugly Betty.”

title: Snoop Dogg Biopic Casts Biggie: D’Angelo and Angie Stone’s Son SwayvoTwain to Play the Notorious B.I.G. (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Universal’s Snoop Dogg biopic is amping up its supporting cast with SwayvoTwain (“Family Legacy,” “Love & Neo-Soul: Honoring the Legacy of D’Angelo”
body:
Universal’s Snoop Dogg biopic is amping up its supporting cast with SwayvoTwain (“Family Legacy,” “Love & Neo-Soul: Honoring the Legacy of D’Angelo”) set to portray Biggie, Bentley Green (“The Land,” “Undercard”) to play RBX and G Perico (“Kings of L.A.,” “She Ball”) as Big Reecie Cup.

	Jonathan Daviss stars in “Snoop,” which is described as the “definitive biopic of the entertainment mogul and icon,” Snoop Dogg. 
	

	Christopher Wallace, aka the Notorious B.I.G., was one of the most influential hip-hop artists of the ’90s and the face of East Coast gangsta rap until his death in 1997. Despite being signed to West Coast powerhouse Death Row Records, Snoop and Biggie shared mutual respect. RBX, whose real name is Eric Dwayne Collins, signed with Death Row in the ’90s alongside his cousin Snoop, launching a rap career that spanned 30 years and multiple hit records. Big Reecie Cup is another key figure in Snoop’s Long Beach roots.


	Craig Brewer (“Hustle and Flow,” “Song Sung Blue”) is directing “Snoop,” which Universal dated for theatrical release on Aug. 6, 2027, based on his rewrite of Joe Robert Cole’s (“Black Panther, “”Wakanda Forever”) original script. 

	The trio of emerging actors add to the film’s starry ensemble, which also features Myles Bullock Be (as Dr. Dre), Lauren London (Snoop’s late mother, Beverly Tate), Camron Jones (Tupac Shakur), Algee Smith (Warren G), Tre Hale (Suge Knight), Laya DeLeon Hayes (Snoop’s wife, Shante Broadus), Olly Sholotan (Kurupt), Corey Champagne (Nate Dogg) and Jonica Booth (The Lady of Rage). 
	

	SwayvoTwain, born Michael D’Angelo Archer II, is a recording artist, songwriter and performer. His parents are the late legendary artists Angie Stone and D’Angelo. His recent music, including “DoveSoar” and “Ms. Angie’s Son,” reflects on their enduring influence while foreshadowing the unique artist SwayvoTwain is becoming, with his blend of Southern soul, hip-hop, melodic R&B and emotionally driven storytelling. “Snoop” marks his first major movie role. He is represented by Mannie House.

	Green began his career as a performer at a young age before transitioning into scripted television, where he made his debut on the popular YouTube series “Epic Rap Battles of History,” portraying a young Michael Jackson and Tootie Ramsey. Since then, he has starred opposite Courtney B. Vance in AMC’s series “61st Street” and with Jack Harlow and Sinqua Walls in the Hulu comedy “White Men Can’t Jump.” His television resume also includes recurring roles in FX’s “Snowfall,” Netflix’s “Mr. Iglesias” and “Sweet Magnolias” and ABCs “The Good Doctor.” Green will next star opposite Wanda Sykes in the feature film “Undercard” and will be featured in Dan Fogelman’s NFL series “The Land” for Hulu. He is represented by Independent Artist Group.

	G Perico is a Los Angeles-based recording artist and actor whose credits include “Kings of L.A.,” “Queen of Manhattan” and “She Ball,” as well as music placements across HBO and Hulu programming. He is represented by Hustle Rite Consulting.

	Snoop Dogg is producing “Snoop,” which will incorporate music from his vast catalog, alongside Imagine Entertainment’s Brian Grazer (“8 Mile”) and Allan Mandelbaum and Death Row Pictures president Sara Ramaker. “Snoop” is the first project under Death Row Pictures’ overall deal with NBCUniversal Entertainment & Studios. Senior VP of production development Ryan Jones and director of development Tony Ducret will oversee the project for the studio.



	

					Bentley Green and G Perico.
									Green: Alan Karuku / Perico: Courtesy of Subject

title: ‘Remain’ Trailer: Jake Gyllenhaal and Phoebe Dynevor Are a Creepy Couple in M. Night Shyamalan’s Latest Twisty Thriller
description:
This Valentine’s Day, be prepared to trust the unknown. 

	M. Night Shyamalan’s romantic drama “Remain” released its first trailer, showing Jake Gyl
body:
This Valentine’s Day, be prepared to trust the unknown. 

	M. Night Shyamalan’s romantic drama “Remain” released its first trailer, showing Jake Gyllenhaal and Phoebe Dynevor in an unsettling relationship.

	The trailer opens with a montage of the happiest moments shared by young couple Wren (Dynevor) and Tate (Gyllenhaal), portraying the film as a seemingly lighthearted romantic comedy. But the tone suddenly shifts when Wren starts to cry while asking, “Why can’t we be together, Tate?” “I think you know,” he whispers back. In the moments that follow, Wren seems to be preparing to slam her head against a bathroom wall before disappearing right in front of Tate. 
	

	Starring alongside Gyllenhaal and Dynevor are Ashley Walters, Julie Hagerty, Jay O. Sanders, Tracy Ifeachor, Hannah James, Caleb Ruminer, Kieran Mulcare and Maria Dizzia. 


	“Remain,” which also inspired author Nicholas Sparks’ novel of the same name, releases in theaters on Valentine’s Day. Shyamalan serves as producer with Ashwin Rajan through Blinding Edge Pictures, alongside Marc Bienstock and Sparks’ producing partner Theresa Park. Sparks executive produces. 

	The film was originally slated for a Halloween 2026 release date before finalizing its Valentine’s Day premiere. Earlier this year, Shyamalan revealed “Remain” was his highest-testing film of his entire career. He’s directed 16 films, including “The Sixth Sense” and “The Visit,” and has written and produced several other thrillers. 

	Shyamalan most recently released “Trap” in 2024, which starred Josh Hartnett as a serial killer who attends a concert with his young daughter, only to realize that police had been tipped off about his presence and the venue was on lockdown. 
	

	Watch the trailer below.

title: Netflix to Report Box Office Numbers for 6 Upcoming Movies as Streamer Escalates Theatrical Plans (EXCLUSIVE)
description: “La Bola Negra” has mucho heat. The generational queer drama swept the Cannes Film Festival off its feet in May, nabbing a $5 million sale to Netfli
body:
“La Bola Negra” has mucho heat. The generational queer drama swept the Cannes Film Festival off its feet in May, nabbing a $5 million sale to Netflix and earning helmers Javier Ambrossi and Javier Calvo the jury prize for best director. After lighting up last weekend’s Telluride Film Festival, the Penélope Cruz-starrer is on its way to Toronto for yet another grand premiere.That’s plenty of bragging rights for an Oscar hopeful, but there’s one more bona fide that has raised eyebrows in the industry: “La Bola Negra” will receive the longest theatrical rollout that Netflix has given any of its films to date. The project has set a 46-day release for Oct. 16, before landing on the Netflix platform on Dec. 2.


	For years, the streamer has engaged in splashy limited releases to hype awards contenders and appease filmmakers who still yearn for the magic of movie theaters. But something about the “La Bola Negra” plan is hitting differently with sources — to say nothing of Netflix’s designs for 2027. That’s when Greta Gerwig’s “Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew” will enjoy a wide release (including Imax screens) for almost 50 days, while the company’s animated “Charlie and the Chocolate Factory” will play wide for 47 days at Christmas. The feeling shared by numerous power players interviewed by Variety is that Netflix — the great Hollywood disruptor — is inching closer to embracing the roughly 130-year tradition of theatrical exhibition. It will also be showing its hand for the first time by reporting box office grosses for a slew of upcoming releases, Variety has learned.
	

	“The real question is ‘What does Netflix want to be now?’” posed one high-level executive at a legacy film studio. “Having almost bought Warner Bros. Discovery, you get the sense that they can’t put some of that toothpaste back in the tube.”
	

	The executive is referring to Netflix’s willingness to own and operate a theatrical distribution entity — as it showed in attempting to acquire Warner Bros. and HBO, until David Ellison’s Paramount swooped in with a larger offer. In a subsequent interview with Bloomberg, Netflix co-CEO Ted Sarandos admitted that he could “see us doing things that we haven’t done before” with movie theaters, but insisted the company was streaming first, as always. For years, Sarandos pooh-poohed the idea of a robust theatrical window, even calling it an “outdated concept” compared with his on-demand and bingeable business model. The numbers seem to back him up. Streaming originals made up 12 of the top 20 most-watched general audience movies around the world this year, per a 2026 report from Nielsen. Thats’ up from seven last year, and includes Netflix’s Matt Damon-Ben Affleck project “The Rip” and “War Machine.”

	The cinema owners, in turn, have done their share of resisting Netflix titles, namely over the company’s refusal to give them a standard period of exclusivity before moving to streaming. COVID- 19 dashed all theatrical hopes when cineplexes were shut down, and the exhibitors have been clawing their way back to normalcy (playing films for 45 days on the big screen before moving them to other windows is the current industry standard). For one of the most deep-pocketed tech monoliths in the world to reconsider, even lightly, its position on theatrical would be a boost, one veteran film distributor says.

	“The exhibitors would absolutely welcome this. Imagine if Netflix of all places threw its weight behind a real theatrical marketing campaign, and not some awards play,” the source said. Though Netflix would be welcomed to the theatrical sandbox, its competitors are insistent that it play by the rules. That means reporting box office grosses, something the data-shy Netflix has never engaged in (to the chagrin of studio and indie distributors). But Netflix will report box office grosses for six upcoming films, two company insiders said: “Narnia” and “Charlie,” as well as “La Bola Negra,” David Fincher’s “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth,” “The Mosquito Bowl” and “Ink.”

	As Netflix and fellow streamers like Apple and Prime Video rose to prominence — largely by overpaying talent with back-end buyouts based on hypothetical box office projections — the establishment fought back by saying the only way to create lasting value for a company’s film library was to eventize each release with major marketing dollars.
	

	Netflix seemed to agree with this, to an extent. Take the eye-popping $450 million it spent in 2021 to acquire the two sequels to Rian Johnson’s “Knives Out” ensemble murder mystery. Part of that deal, Variety reported at the time, entailed tens of millions of dollars in marketing spending to make the films feel as big as theatrical debuts. Netflix fulfilled its promise to spend big, but many industry observers said the company left a ton of cash on the table by skipping cinemas. The same was said in 2024 of the Jason Bateman thriller “Carry-On,” the third-most-watched film ever on the service.

	Theatrical distribution at Netflix has been headed by Spencer Klein since 2019. The former 20th Century Fox steward, who booked releases for juggernauts like the “Deadpool” and “Planet of the Apes” franchises, also dates movies on the service and manages Netflix-owned theaters in New York and Los Angeles. He also guided Netflix to its first No. 1 box office weekend in August 2025, with a sing-along version of its animated Oscar winner “KPop Demon Hunters.” Klein is respected among his peers and will be watched closely as “Narnia” and “Charlie” start ramping up.

	Those inside Netflix, per individuals with close knowledge of the company, are downplaying the significance of this theatrical flirtation. Extending big-screen runs, as the company line often goes, is part of a bespoke process where the film team decides “what’s right” for each movie.

schema.headline: Netflix to Report Box Office Numbers for 6 Upcoming Movies as Streamer Escalates Theatrical Plans (EXCLUSIVE)

title: Broadcast Networks Fire Up San Sebastián
description: Atresmedia Cine heads to San Sebastián with four films across key festival sections: “El mal padre” in the main competition, “La Bola Negra” in Perl
body:
Atresmedia Cine heads to San Sebastián with four films across key festival sections: “El mal padre” in the main competition, “La Bola Negra” in Perlak (Atresmedia Cine has acquired free-to-air rights to the buzzy drama), “Karateka” at the Velodrome and “Blind Ants” (“Inurri Itsuak”), which opens Zinemira. Atresmedia Group will also present the series “Sira” and “Trazos ocultos.”

	That breadth reflects the company’s role in Spanish film, says Jaime Ortiz de Artiñano, managing director of Atresmedia Cine. “The presence of four films and two series at this year’s San Sebastián Festival demonstrates the strength of a model that drives ambitious projects and accompanies them all the way to their encounters with audiences,” he says.
	

	San Sebastián is also a strategic launchpad. Ortiz de Artiñano calls it “one of the great international showcases for our cinema,” as well as “the starting point for many of our campaigns,” where Atresmedia begins building conversation around upcoming releases.


	Atresmedia’s current strategy spans established franchises such as “Torrente Presidente,” large-scale productions including “Karateka” and “La Bola Negra,” and “El mal padre,” but all share “ambition, personality and the ability to move and connect,” says Ortiz de Artiñano. 

	That audience focus is central to his view of Spanish cinema’s next phase. “The future of Spanish cinema does not lie in making more films, but in getting more people to want to see them,” he says.

	Platforms are increasingly part of that equation. Ortiz de Artiñano points to Movistar Plus’ Original “La Bola Negra” and Netflix’s involvement in “Karateka” as examples of partnerships that help make more ambitious Spanish films possible.

schema.headline: Broadcast Networks Fire Up San Sebastián

title: Broadcasters and Streamers Move From Rivals to Partners as Old TV Divide Breaks Down and YouTube Rises Fast – Lumiere Summit
description: For most of the past decade, television’s defining battle was broadcasters versus streamers. Now that divide is breaking down fast, as traditional T
body:
For most of the past decade, television’s defining battle was broadcasters versus streamers. Now that divide is breaking down fast, as traditional TV groups – who’ve seen linear advertising and viewing fall – are now keen to collaborate with global streamers to continue financing ambitious content and gain some scale. 

	Few deals illustrate the shift better than TF1’s decision to put its channels and AVOD service TF1+ inside Netflix. TF1+ already reaches around 42 million people a month, while TF1 President Rodolphe Belmer said the broadcaster estimates Netflix has roughly 14 million members in France, many of whom increasingly use it as their first destination for television. 
	

	“The more Netflix is growing, the more our addressable market in consequence is shrinking, and the more our ability to amortize our lineup of content and to finance our shows is under stress,” Belmer said. “And evidently, to tackle all that, we had to take the decision to distribute our lineup of content on Netflix to be able to reach Netflix members and advertise our content on the wider possible perimeter of French audiences.”


	Belmer was speaking at the Lumière Summit in Saint-Paul-de-Vence alongside Prime Video executive Andrew Bennett, Globo CEO Paulo Marinho and Gaumont Television chief Isabelle Degeorges on a panel exploring the increasingly intertwined relationship between broadcasters and streamers.

	For Amazon, aggregation has always been a core part of the business.

	“We have been both a programmer and an aggregator since our inception,” Bennett said. “We were an SVOD, TVOD, then we were SVOD, TVOD, channels, now we’re SVOD, TVOD, free-to-air. It is foundational to our strategy to bring all of the selection together in one app.”
	

	He pointed to Prime Video partnerships with France Télévisions, M6, Spain’s RTVE and Germany’s ARD and ZDF. In Europe in particular, he said, local programming has become indispensable.

	“Particularly in Europe, it’s very clear to me now you cannot be successful without significant disproportionate amounts of local programming,” Bennett said. “It’s what customers want. It’s what they’re accustomed to.”

	Globo, meanwhile, offers another version of the model. The Brazilian giant spans free-to-air television, pay TV, Globoplay, production and sports, reaching some 120 million people weekly, with a major novela capable of attracting around 40 million viewers per episode. 

	Marinho said Globo remains committed to its own ecosystem but left open the possibility of deeper partnerships with global platforms.

	“I never say never because the market’s shifting and changing so fast,” he said. “It’s a possibility. I would say not for now, but maybe advancing and having part of our streaming content, sharing window, sharing advertisement would be a first step.”

	Advertising sits at the heart of those decisions. As broadcasters distribute more content through third-party platforms, the question is no longer simply who reaches the viewer, but who controls the commercial relationship around that viewer.

	Marinho said Globo wants to preserve its direct relationship with advertisers even when working with outside distributors. “In terms of advertisement, we try to control the relationship with the market,” he said. “And some discussions that we might have around the distribution monetization is always a very important part of the discussion. Who and how you’re going to monetize this inventory and the data piece as well.”

	For Belmer, audience data has become particularly important for targeted advertising. European regulation, he argued, has focused heavily on whether broadcasters remain visible on connected devices but not enough on who controls consumer consent and the information needed to monetize those audiences.

	“It is absolutely crucial for the monetization of content long-term,” he said.

	But the panel drew a distinction between data as a commercial asset and data as a creative tool.
	

	Degeorges said producers remain largely shut out from much of the audience information generated by the platforms carrying their shows.

	“We don’t know. I mean, as producer, we don’t have any data,” she said.

	Belmer argued that broadcasters have spent decades commissioning without direct access to individual viewer data.

	“We continue to do our shows with instincts, with our understanding of the French population, and also resorting to measurement panels,” he said.

	While acknowledging he wasn’t working on originals, Bennett refuted claims that Prime Video may be relying on data too heavily to develop shows. “Creativity is not something that data – it’s generally backward-looking, and creativity is forward-looking,” he said. “No data is going to tell you the alchemy of a director and a cast and music and casting.”

	The convergence of broadcasters and streamers is also changing one of streaming’s original defining principles – exclusivity.

	“Exclusive, not exclusive, first window, second window, that’s just a function of the relationship between your investment level and where you think the outcome will be in terms of what you think is a good investment or a bad investment,” Bennett said. “But we don’t obsess about one size fits all.”

	Belmer said TF1 already shares roughly 15 shows a year with streamers under different arrangements. Sometimes a partner gets the first window and TF1 the second; in other cases, the shows launch day-and-date.

	“What we have experienced, the level of cannibalization is relatively moderate,” Belmer said. “It means that it makes sense for us, financially speaking, to do this kind of deals with our partners.”

	Ten weeks into the partnership with Netflix, the feared cannibalization of TF1+ has proved surprisingly limited. “For the moment, the cannibalization is very, very small, less than 10%,” Belmer said. “Much, much smaller than what we modelized when we did the partnership.”

	For producers, however, greater flexibility around distribution only works if they retain enough long-term value.

	Degeorges made clear that IP ownership remains fundamental to Gaumont.

	“If we don’t have the IPs, yes, we get money to make the show, we get money for our companies, but at the end of the day, we don’t have any rights,” she said. “Because the IP is our library, our availability to create, to develop, to just move forward with our companies.”
	

	She said French regulation now allows producers to retain IP in roughly 70% of cases. 

	Ultimately, Degeorges acknowledged there is a risk of European producers and broadcasters becoming increasingly dependent on U.S. platforms to finance local creation.

	“Yes, I mean, it is a risk,” she said. “We know that. That’s why our government, everybody, has to fight. Us, we have to fight to remain, to keep this sovereignty.”

	“We also have to fight for the investors in public audiovisual because they make a lot of shows and we need these shows,” she said. Her hope, she added, is that partnerships ultimately allow the industry to make “more shows, more diverse shows, more volume” while maintaining a viable domestic production ecosystem.

	If broadcasters and streamers are becoming increasingly interdependent, YouTube may be giving them another reason to find common ground.

	“I think that it’s absolutely necessary that YouTube gets regulated,” Belmer said. “All of us, broadcasters, streamers, we are in France and in many European countries heavily regulated. Today, as you said, YouTube has established itself on the TV screen, and it is competing for the same market as we are without any regulation.”

	Belmer argued that the imbalance is especially stark because global subscription streamers have already been incorporated into France’s cultural financing system.

	Amazon, Netflix and Disney, he said, “are good citizens of the French cultural exception, very good citizens. And they finance cinema, they finance shows, they play by the same rules as all of us.”

	Netflix, Prime Video and Disney+ are currently challenging a newer diversity requirement layered onto France’s existing streaming investment regime. The three platforms have separately appealed a sub-quota requiring them to devote 20% of their mandatory audiovisual investment to genres including animation, documentaries and recorded or recreated live performance. 

	The lobbying push is mounting as the European Commission prepares to review the Audiovisual Media Services Directive which sets guidelines for streamers’ investment in European content. 

	Belmer said YouTube is already capturing a significant share of the TV advertising market without carrying comparable local investment obligations. He said the platform can sell advertising at prices 2.5 to three times below those of traditional broadcasters, describing those prices as “predatory.”
	

	Degeorges made the producer argument in broader terms.

	“You get money from creation, and YouTube gets a lot of money from creation because they distribute channels, they distribute creators, they distribute a lot of French content which have been financed by our ecosystem,” she said.

	 “In our system, actors who get money from creation have to finance creation. I mean, it’s very simple,” Degeorges said.

schema.headline: Broadcasters and Streamers Move From Rivals to Partners as Old TV Divide Breaks Down and YouTube Rises Fast – Lumiere Summit

title: ‘Snowfall’ Spinoff ‘The Drop’ Is an Evocative, If Uneven, Portrait of South L.A. in the Gangsta Rap Era: TV Review
description: The FX drama “Snowfall” was one of the sneak success stories of the Peak TV era. Co-created by a marquee film director in “Boyz N the Hood” auteur J
body:
The FX drama “Snowfall” was one of the sneak success stories of the Peak TV era. Co-created by a marquee film director in “Boyz N the Hood” auteur John Singleton, “Snowfall” thrived where many series of similar origin failed. But it did so quietly: “Snowfall” didn’t win awards or mint breakouts beyond lead actor Damson Idris, but after premiering in 2017 — before the launch of Apple TV or Disney+, and an eternity ago in Hollywood years — the crime show steadily grew for six seasons before concluding in 2023, a rarity for an original drama these days.
	

	Three years later, “Snowfall” has received another accolade that testifies to its under-heralded success: a spinoff. Beginning in 1990, four years after the final episodes of its parent show, “The Drop: A Snowfall Saga” retains the South Los Angeles setting, but shifts its focus from the drug trade amid the rise of crack cocaine to the music industry amid the rise of gangsta rap. Instead of a West Coast version of “The Wire” or “Narcos,” “The Drop” is more like a fictionalized version of N.W.A biopic “Straight Outta Compton.” (There’s a nod to the late group member Eazy-E in the opening minutes.)


	While “The Drop” doesn’t craft its protagonists into figures as compelling as Dr. Dre, Ice Cube or Snoop Dogg, the world they navigate is instilled with a vivid sense of place. It’s rare for productions to film in L.A. these days, let alone celebrate the city to the extent “The Drop” does. That’s a quality worth admiring, even if the series can be uneven in its early episodes.
	

	The connective tissue between “Snowfall” and “The Drop” is heroine Wanda (Gail Bean), a recovering addict set on improving her lot in life, and her ex-boyfriend Leon (Isaiah John), a reformed dealer initially tangential to the plot until Wanda ropes him into her master plan. (“The Drop” creator Malcolm Spellman, previously of the Disney+ Marvel series “The Falcon and the Winter Soldier,” never worked on “Snowfall.”) Wanda’s vision is to creatively matchmake her 19-year-old cousin Lamarr (Asante Blackk), a budding producer, with buzzy rapper Artillery (Simmie Sims III, himself an MC who performs under the stage name Buddy), whose latest underground single controversially crows over a police officer killed in the line of duty.

	Watching Wanda scramble her way up the industry ladder, managing her charges and sweet-talking gatekeepers, gives “The Drop” its skeleton. “Atlanta,” another FX show about the rap game and its pitfalls as experienced by two cousins, almost took its main characters’ upward trajectory for granted, letting their ascendance play out in the background while episodes focused on smaller scenarios. “The Drop” takes a more linear approach as Wanda lobbies money man Darryl (Brandon Mychal Smith) for a job as an A&R executive and label boss Jenny (Isidora Goreshter) to put Artillery’s song on the radio. When Wanda applies the principles of drug distribution —  let customers sample the product for free, and they’ll pay for more if it’s good — to putting out a tape, it’s a clever callback to “Snowfall.”

	Inexplicably, though, “The Drop” neglects key players in the music business story for family strife that can’t match the intrigue of the rap game. Artillery, who’s being hunted down by vindictive cops, rightly accuses Lamar of caring more about sourcing vocals than his physical safety. But “The Drop” is guilty of the same tunnel vision; besides Artillery’s gang affiliation with the Bloods, whose escalating conflict with the Crips makes everyday life increasingly violent even for civilian bystanders, we learn almost nothing about him as a person in the first five episodes. Instead, “The Drop” is focused on how the death of Lamar’s mother, once a musician herself, affected him and his older brother, James (Peyton Alex Smith). The siblings were raised by their grandparents, laundromat owner Big Daddy (Mykelti Williamson) and his wife, Gerty (Nicki Micheaux), the latter of whom is firmly against Lamar and her niece Wanda chasing the dream she still blames for the family’s loss.
	

	“The Drop” spends an entire episode teasing out the backstory behind this shared wound. While a well-liked actor from another prestige cable show makes an appearance as Lamar and James’ late mother in a pleasant surprise I won’t spoil, nothing revealed about the household’s family dynamics is as intriguing as the period detail in the flashbacks. An opening scene of a tent revival in 1950s L.A. gives way to the Afros and wide lapels of the 1970s, skipping through generations of Black migration, religion and musical tradition. There’s no reason “The Drop” couldn’t use other storylines as a vehicle for such anthropology, especially with underdeveloped figures like Artillery or Jenny — an L.A. native waging an uphill battle to modernize her dad’s company — standing on the sidelines.

	That the scenery can be so much more intriguing than the action in the foreground is a recurring problem with “The Drop,” but also a testament to its strengths. Like any story about fictitious talents, “The Drop” can strain to position its original music as a world-altering invention; Wanda posits that a single heavily sampling Chaka Khan’s “Ain’t Nobody” is the kind of uniting force that could end gang warfare, an eyebrow-raising idea. But I had no trouble believing the palm-lined streets, Craftsman houses and sunbaked concrete were the same ingredients that gave rise to a massively influential art form. If “The Drop” can get its plot to the level of its immersive production, it’ll be something to see.

	“The Drop” premieres on FX and Hulu on Sep. 8 at 9pm ET, with remaining episodes airing weekly on Tuesdays.

schema.headline: ‘Snowfall’ Spinoff ‘The Drop’ Is an Evocative, If Uneven, Portrait of South L.A. in the Gangsta Rap Era: TV Review

title: Inside Rauw Alejandro’s Three-Act Concert in New York, a Celebration of Music, Culture and Puerto Rican Pride: ‘It Creates an Impact on All Latinos to Embrace Their Culture’
description: Amid a political climate that has seen Latino communities targeted by deportations and ICE raids and the polarizing effects of gentrification and po
body:
Amid a political climate that has seen Latino communities targeted by deportations and ICE raids and the polarizing effects of gentrification and poverty in Puerto Rico, Latin music artists such as Rauw Alejandro and Bad Bunny have responded with a renewed sense of cultural pride and advocacy.

	Both artists released their most personal albums within weeks of each other: Alejandro’s fifth studio album, “Cosa Nuestra,” came out in November 2024, and Bad Bunny’s “Debí Tirar Más Fotos” followed in January 2025 — and of course Bad Bunny followed with not only a sold-out residency in Puerto Rico followed by a world tour, but his multiple Emmy-winning Super Bowl halftime show.
	

	Alejandro has followed as well, with 2025’s “Cosa Nuestra: Capítulo 0” and a two-night stand at New York’s Forest Hills Stadium this past weekend — making him the first Latin artist to headline the iconic venue, which over the years has hosted the Beatles, Bob Dylan, Frank Sinatra, the Rolling Stones, Jimi Hendrix and countless others. It’s all part of an effort to encourage Latinos to embrace their roots and identities with greater pride.


	“I think that creates an impact on all Latinos to embrace their culture, to not be afraid of showing their real identity. You don’t have to hide from nobody,” Alejandro — born Raúl Alejandro Ocasio Ruiz — told Variety during rehearsals at Forest Hills Stadium on Friday. “I think that’s what ‘Cosa Nuestra’ and ‘Debí Tirar Más Fotos’ did. It’s always been with us in a way. Getting older and more mature as an artist, you keep evolving.”
	



	

									DREW GURIAN
	



	His shows at the venue, titled “Red Bull Chapters With Rauw Alejandro,” made that pride even more explicit. The production was designed to educate audiences about and celebrate Puerto Rico and its diaspora, including those who call cities like New York home.

	When Alejandro launched his “Cosa Nuestra” tour in 2025, it also marked a rebranding for the artist — one that redefines his identity beyond being a reggaeton star, a singer or dancer. The shows were the two-time Latin Grammy winner’s first of 2026, and the energy drink brand’s first concert of its kind.

	The three-part show took fans through Alejandro’s musical evolution, tracing his path toward becoming the artist he once dreamed of being while paying homage to the influences that shaped him.

	“Three chapters is very little to tell a whole story, but I think we came up with a nice idea: briefing a little bit and just focusing on giving a nice message to our fans,” he says. Through cultural symbolism, powerful speeches about Latino identity and meticulously crafted choreography, the 90-minute show unfolded in three chapters: Inspiration, Momentum and Legacy. Puerto Rican pride remained the show’s central theme, with graphics and stage designs depicting different parts of the island and New York City — two places that shaped his childhood.

	“I think it’s really important that we create a whole movement putting Puerto Rico and our culture on the world stage,” Alejandro says. “I think there’s room for everybody to do it. There are people who did it before us, and this new generation deserves to connect again with their roots. New York and P.R. for me are really special. My father is from Brooklyn and Puerto Rican as well, from Canóvanas. My mom is from Carolina, so it’s home.”

	While he performed, the visuals in Chapter 1 included the island’s beaches, colorful architecture and red, white and celestial-blue flag, the original colors it held before the island became U.S. Territory. The show began with a narration describing the formative elements of the artist’s life: where he lived, the people who surrounded him and the childhood experiences that influenced his musical taste and motivated him to pursue his dreams. He opened with his hit “Santa,” followed by a medley of “Dream Girl” and “Toda.” Next came “Déjame Entrar,” before he transitioned into his rendition of salsa pioneer Frankie Ruiz’s 1985 hit “Tú Con Él.”
	

	To close the show’s first arc, Alejandro sang “Carita Linda” as skateboarders performed onstage wearing helmets and costumes inspired by Puerto Rico’s vejigantes, folkloric masked characters with multiple horns and exaggerated facial features who appear at carnivals and festivals throughout the island.

	Chapter 2 portrayed Alejandro’s transition into life as a famous Latin music star navigating the pressures, routines and chameleon-like shifts of a successful career. The visuals evolved into the New York City skyline, which also appeared throughout the production, making it clear that he intended to create a visual love letter to the Puerto Rican diaspora. Songs from his 2021 album “Vice Versa” and his 2022 release “Playa Saturno” were performed, including “Todo de Ti,” “Baby Hello,” “Desenfocao’” and the remix of “Tiroteo.”

	For Chapter 3, Alejandro honored the legendary artists who made reggaeton a global genre. The singer brought out music producer Tainy onstage as the evening’s first guest. He ran through a reggaeton canon that included music by Héctor el Father, Daddy Yankee, Arcángel, Tony Dize and Bad Bunny — artists who helped establish reggaeton as a global, chart-topping genre. Chencho Corleone, one-half of the reggaeton duo Plan B, then joined Alejandro for “El Efecto” and “Desesperados,” before the show closed with “Lokera” and “Punto 40.”

	“I think this new generation deserves to connect again with the roots, and I think that’s the important thing, that we keep growing,” said Rauw. “These kids don’t know who the pioneers are, and I think it’s our responsibility to show them and educate them to see what’s up.”



	

					Rauw Alejandro at Red Bull Chapters in Queens, New York, USA on September 5, 2026.
									FAITH NGUYEN

title: Danielle Deadwyler, Ike Barinholtz and Connor Storrie Join Billie Eilish and Carey Mulligan in ‘The Bell Jar’
description:
Focus Features has confirmed the cast for Academy Award winner Sarah Polley‘s “The Bell Jar,” starring Billie Eilish. 

	Eilish, a two-time Oscar-wi
body:
Focus Features has confirmed the cast for Academy Award winner Sarah Polley‘s “The Bell Jar,” starring Billie Eilish. 

	Eilish, a two-time Oscar-winning singer-songwriter, makes her film acting debut playing Esther Greenwood, the protagonist of Sylvia Plath’s classic novel. Plath’s semi-autobiographical story follows as the aspiring young writer landes a magazine internship in New York City and chronicles her struggles with ambition, identity and mental health amid the stifling societal expectations for women in the 1950s.
	

	Production has wrapped on the film, which Polley (“Women Talking”) directed from her own adapted screenplay. The filmmaker assembled an acclaimed supporting cast to join Eilish, including Oscar- and Emmy-nominee Carey Mulligan, whom Variety exclusively reported signed on to play Esther’s mother, Mrs. Greenwood.  


	Also confirmed to star are Gotham Award winner Danielle Deadwyler as Dr. Nolan, Esther’s psychiatrist; Actor Award winner Ike Barinholtz as Lenny, a wealthy NYC radio host; and “Heated Rivalry” breakout Connor Storrie as Marco, whom Esther is set up with on a horrifying blind date. Dylan Hawco (as Buddy Willard, Esther’s first boyfriend), Lili Taylor (Jay Cee, editor of Ladies’ Day magazine), Ella Beatty (Joan, an old acquaintance who ends up at the same mental hospital as Esther) and Maggie Kuntz (Doreen, Esther’s best friend in New York and a fellow intern) are also featured in the ensemble cast.

	“The Bell Jar” is produced by Plan B, Studiocanal and Joy Coalition. Focus will distribute the film, with a release date to be announced. 
	

	Polley is represented by WME, GGA, and Circle Management + Production and Eilish is represented by WME, Sandbox Entertainment, High Rise PR and Gang, Tyre, Ramer, Brown & Passman, Inc. 

	Mulligan is represented by Julian Belfrage, CAA, and Jackoway Austen et al; Deadwyler is represented by Paradigm, Play Management and Ziffren Brittenham; Barinholtz is represented by UTA, Artists First, and Jared Levine from Morris Yorn Barnes Levine Krintzman Rubenstein Kohner & Gellman; and Storrie is represented by CAA, Linden Entertainment, Shelter PR, and Yorn Levine.

	Hawco is represented by GGA, Gersh and Circle Management + Production; Taylor is represented by Independent Artist Group, Untitled Entertainment and Schreck, Rose, Dapello, Adams, Berlin & Dunham; Beatty is represented by Entertainment 360 and CAA; and Kuntz is represented by Verve and The Rozenzweig Group. 



	

					Dylan Hawco, Lili Taylor, Ella Beatty and Maggie Kuntz.

title: Third Person Dies at Burning Man
description:
Burning Man
                          Death Toll Climbs To 3
body:
Burning Man
                          Death Toll Climbs To 3
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              September 8, 2026
                            10:59 AM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            A third person has died at the Burning Man festival in Nevada.
      
    
            The Pershing County Sheriff's Office confirmed the third death on Monday -- the 2026 edition's final day.
      
    
            Authorities have only said the attendee died while on the way to a hospital in Reno. They provided no further information.
      

            As we've reported ... the first attendee, Sampson Tshombe, was pronounced dead at the festival on September 3 after a sudden illness. He was treated with lifesaving measures before being transported to the festival's emergency care center, where he was pronounced dead.
      
    
            Dispatch was notified Saturday about another possible death. After arriving on the scene, deputies were told a man -- identified as Craig Mann -- had been found dead in his trailer.
      
    
            The medical examiner's office is conducting autopsies for both Tshombe and Mann. It's unclear if they'll do the same for the third person who died, but it seems likely.
      
    
            Pershing County Sheriff Jerry Allen noted the festival usually averages just 1 death per year ... making the death toll in 2026 highly unusual.

                          Allegedly Shoved Girlfriend and Put His Han
body:
Jack Doherty Battery Arrest
                          Allegedly Shoved Girlfriend and Put His Hands Around Her Neck
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              September 8, 2026
                            10:35 AM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Jack Doherty's domestic battery arrest was allegedly scarier than originally thought ... cops say the popular YouTuber's girlfriend claims he pushed her down and wrapped his hands around her neck, prompting her to grab a gun to protect herself.
      
    
            The probable cause affidavit, obtained by TMZ, lays out all the allegations against Jack, who cops say got into a heated argument Friday afternoon with his girlfriend inside a Florida home.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Cops say the woman told officers Jack ran up to her and got right in her face during a confrontation, scaring the heck out of her. As a result, the woman says she used her arm to put some distance between her and Jack.
      

            According to the affidavit, the two continued to argue as the woman went upstairs to gather her things to leave the residence. The woman claims Jack was super pissed that she was trying to make a quick exit and "pushed her to the ground and used his hands around her neck to briefly pin her to the ground."
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            She told police she was able to breathe despite Jack's hands around her throat, but said she still grabbed a firearm from a bedside table and threatened to shoot him if he came near her again.
      
    
            Cops responded to a 911 call for a domestic disturbance, and police ended up arresting Jack for misdemeanor domestic battery.
      
    
            Sources close to Jack previously told us he acted in self-defense.
